# Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?

Zijian Liu, Yangzhixin Luo, Junyu Lu, Yi Li, Yu Chen, David Xu, William
F. Shen, Xinchi Qiu, Xisen Wang University of Oxford (ox.ac.uk) King
Abdullah University of Science and Technology (kaust.edu.sa) University
of Sydney (usyd.edu.au) University of Cambridge (cam.ac.uk)

###### Abstract

Multi-agent AI scientists have shown improving performance across a
diverse range of tasks. Yet a common approach is design-time agentic
orchestration, which typically relies on fixed workflows. In contrast,
human scientists coordinate and adjust their division of labor at
runtime. We therefore ask: can AI scientists also coordinate at runtime?
To this end, we introduce Runtime Agent Coordination (RAC), which
selects agents from existing AI-scientist hosts during execution,
assigns scoped work contracts, and provides artifact-grounded
verification. Verification informs subsequent agents without blocking
transitions or discarding artifacts. We conduct a single-seed
exploratory evaluation across Agent Laboratory, EvoScientist, and ARK on
ResearchClawBench, preserving host models, tools, and permissions under
host-calibrated budgets. Four cumulative conditions separate native
execution, runtime communication, runtime selection, and the combined
addition of contracts and verification. Runtime selection yields the
highest observed mean score for each host; adding contracts and
verification reduces these means, with host-dependent outcomes relative
to native execution. These results motivate runtime coordination while
exposing the limits of additional coordination mechanisms under
constrained budgets. Code is available at
[https://github.com/systemind-team/Runtime-AI-Scientist](https://github.com/systemind-team/Runtime-AI-Scientist).

## 1 Introduction

AI scientists automate increasingly large parts of the research
lifecycle, including idea generation, literature synthesis, experiment
design, implementation, analysis, and paper writing ([Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Schmidgall et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Goel et al., 2025](#bib.bib19); [Gottweis et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)). Multi-agent systems
distribute these activities across specialized roles that exchange
prompts, critiques, code, and research artifacts. This communication
determines what agents share. Coordination is a separate decision: which
agent should act next, what it should produce, whether its output is
valid, and how the run should continue.

Many prominent AI-scientist systems organize agent interactions through
predefined stages, loops, and fallback rules ([Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Xin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)). Search, repair, and debate add flexibility within
these workflows, but do not necessarily let the system select the most
relevant agent across stages ([Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Liu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib18)). Other systems, such as EvoScientist ([Lyu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib24)), incorporate persistent memory and
self-evolution. These differences motivate us to investigate whether a
shared runtime coordination approach can improve research performance
across hosts with varying degrees of native flexibility.

Selecting the next agent based on the current research state matters
because long-horizon scientific failures are state dependent. A missing
result calls for an experimenter, a broken bibliography calls for a
deterministic check or writer, or a contradictory figure may require
code rather than another prose revision. Recent evaluations locate
substantial AI-scientist failures in experimental design, grounding, and
scientific reasoning rather than only in software crashes ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10); [Fei et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). A fixed workflow
cannot remove these failures merely by adding more agents. It must
either execute all contingencies, which increases cost, or omit
contingencies that later turn out to be necessary.

We therefore ask whether runtime coordination is a useful alternative to
fixed workflows for multi-agent AI scientists ([Wang,
2026](#bib.bib25)). To address this question, we propose Runtime Agent
Coordination (RAC), illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?"),
which uses current artifacts, open problems, execution history, and
remaining budget to select an authorized existing agent. Scoped
contracts define what each selected agent should accomplish, while
artifact-grounded verification provides feedback on its output for
subsequent work. Every verdict retains the workspace and host
transition. We apply the same framework across different hosts under
matched budgets, keeping their underlying agents and tools fixed to
assess the benefits of communication and coordination.

Our core contributions are threefold. First, we formally study runtime
coordination in multi-agent AI scientists and formulate next-agent
selection as a state-dependent decision, distinguishing it from
communication under native workflow control. Second, we instantiate the
RAC framework in multi-agent AI scientists such as Agent Laboratory,
EvoScientist, and ARK without replacing their native agents, tools, or
permissions. Third, we empirically test whether runtime coordination
improves research performance under matched budgets, reporting research
scores, token usage, and estimated inference costs across a range of
tasks.

![Refer to caption](2610.00980v1/figure1_overview_revised.png)

Figure 1: Same agents, different coordination. (a) Native transitions
versus state-dependent selection by the current agent, with inter-agent

based on current state, without a separate orchestrator; returned
artifacts update the state for the next decision. (d) The cumulative
conditions add communication (R1), runtime selection (R2), and contracts
plus verification (R3) to the native lifecycle (N0).

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 AI Scientists

AI scientists aim to automate research activities ranging from idea
generation and experimentation to analysis and scientific writing ([Lu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Tang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib17)). The AI Scientist organizes these activities
into an end-to-end workflow, while AI Scientist-v2 introduces agentic
tree search within experimentation ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1);
[Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)). Agent Laboratory assigns specialized
agents to research phases, AI-Researcher combines literature exploration
with experimental development, and ARK provides a human-steered research
harness ([Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Xin et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)). These systems
demonstrate different ways to organize specialized capabilities across
the research lifecycle.

Other systems emphasize iterative feedback and adaptation. Co-scientist
combines hypothesis generation, debate, and ranking ([Gottweis et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)); AutoResearchClaw integrates multi-agent debate,
execution repair, and verifiable reporting ([Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18)); and ARIS uses cross-model review and evidence checks
to assess research claims ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)). EvoScientist
accumulates reusable research experience through persistent memory and
self-evolution ([Lyu et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)). Moving beyond
predefined pipelines, freephdlabor supports workflows determined by
real-time agent reasoning, while AutoScientists organizes decentralized
teams around evolving experimental evidence ([Li et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7); [Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). Our work examines
whether a shared runtime coordination approach can improve existing
hosts with different native control mechanisms.

Scientific output also requires evaluation beyond successful execution.
ResearchClawBench evaluates end-to-end research on real-paper-derived
tasks, while diagnostic studies examine failures in experimental design,
grounding, and scientific reasoning ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib10); [Fei
et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). Automated review introduces further
uncertainty because assessments can vary across evaluator
models ([Ravideshik and Kejriwal, 2026](#bib.bib15)). We therefore
distinguish feedback used during research from external benchmark
evaluation of the final outputs.

### 2.2 Multi-Agent Coordination

Multi-agent systems combine specialized roles through communication and
structured collaboration. AutoGen supports programmable agent
conversations, MetaGPT combines role-specific workflows with shared
structured messages, and multi-agent debate iteratively exchanges
candidate answers and critiques ([Wu et al., 2023](#bib.bib20); [Hong et
al., 2023](#bib.bib21); [Du et al., 2023](#bib.bib22)). These mechanisms
shape the information available to agents, while coordination determines
how their contributions are organized and which agent acts next.

Several approaches explicitly optimize or adapt this organization.
GPTSwarm represents agents as computational graphs and optimizes prompts
and inter-agent connectivity ([Zhuge et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)). DyLAN
selects agent teams and supports dynamic interactions during task
solving ([Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib9)). In scientific applications,
freephdlabor and AutoScientists further demonstrate reasoning-driven
workflows and self-organizing collaboration ([Li et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7); [Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). Building on these
directions, RAC studies runtime selection across existing AI-scientist
hosts while preserving their underlying agents, tools, and permissions.
Its cumulative conditions distinguish communication under native control
from runtime selection and the combined addition of contracts and
verification.

Feedback and resource use are integral to this comparison. MetaGPT
incorporates executable feedback, while analyses of multi-agent failures
identify inter-agent misalignment and verification or termination
problems ([Hong et al., 2023](#bib.bib21); [Cemri et al.,
2025](#bib.bib14)). In RAC, scoped contracts define the selected agent’s
task, and artifact-grounded verification informs subsequent work without
vetoing transitions. Because additional coordination can increase
inference costs, we follow cost-aware agent evaluation
principles ([Kapoor et al., 2024](#bib.bib12); [Kapoor et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13)) and compare research scores, token usage, and
estimated costs under matched run-level budgets.

## 3 Runtime Agent Coordination for AI Scientists

### 3.1 Problem Formulation

At decision step $`t`$, an AI scientist has a research state $`s_{t}`$
comprising its current objective, saved artifacts, unresolved problems,
execution history, and remaining budget. Let $`\mathcal{A}_{t}`$ denote
the agents currently permitted by the host. Communication adds
information to this state, while runtime coordination uses it to select
the next agent and specify its task. At a nonterminal handoff, the next
agent is selected as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
a_{t+1}=\begin{cases}\pi_{\mathrm{host}}(s_{t}),&\text{native control (N0, R1)},\\[3.0pt]
\pi_{\mathrm{RAC}}(s_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t}),&\text{runtime coordination (R2, R3)},\end{cases}\qquad a_{t+1}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}.
``` |  | (1) |

Here, $`\pi_{\mathrm{host}}`$ is the host’s native successor policy, and
$`\pi_{\mathrm{RAC}}`$ is the shared runtime selection policy. Native
policies may already include conditional branches, fallback rules, or
adaptive delegation. Our comparison examines the effect of replacing
this native selection policy with a shared state-dependent policy while
retaining the host’s permitted agents. Each condition generates its own
research trajectory, so $`s_{t}`$ need not be identical across
conditions.

### 3.2 Engineering Implementation

Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Engineering Implementation ‣ 3 Runtime Agent Coordination for AI Scientists ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
summarizes the execution cycle. We use the same RAC package and
condition configuration across Agent Laboratory, EvoScientist, and ARK.
Each host bridge serializes native state, invokes an existing
capability, and returns artifacts and usage records through a shared
interface. Bridges contain no host-specific runtime selection rules,
verification criteria, or benchmark hints. This design preserves each
host’s agents, tools, and permissions without requiring identical host
internals.

Figure 2: The RAC execution cycle. At each handoff, agents exchange
requests and results. In R2–R3, the current agent selects the next
authorized host capability from a fresh checkpoint, without a separate
orchestrator. R3 additionally specifies a work contract and verifies the
returned artifacts, passing feedback to the next selected agent.

N0 executes the host-native lifecycle without additional communication
mechanisms or a RAC phase loop. R1 introduces inter-agent communication
while preserving the native successor at every handoff. R2 retains this
communication mechanism and enables the current agent to select the next
authorized capability using artifacts, execution history, unresolved
problems, and remaining budget. Agents exchange structured requests and
results through a common communication channel. Thus, R1–R2 changes
next-agent selection while retaining the same communication mechanism.
Communication state is isolated between runs, and cross-run memory is
reset across all conditions.

R3 adds scoped work contracts and artifact-grounded verification. Each
contract specifies the objective, readable and writable artifacts, and
required output. The verifier checks persisted artifacts against the
contract and records a supported, refuted, or inconclusive verdict. All
verdicts preserve the workspace and host transition; feedback enters the
next selected agent’s prompt rather than directly triggering retries,
rerouting, rollback, or stopping. Runs terminate on budget exhaustion,
hard hop limits, terminal provider errors, or native host completion.
Checkpoints and event records document coordination decisions, while
external benchmark evaluation assesses final outputs separately from
in-loop verification.

## 4 Experimental Setup

### 4.1 Baselines

We evaluated RAC with Agent Laboratory ([Schmidgall et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3)), EvoScientist ([Lyu et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)), and
ARK ([Xin et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)). These hosts span predefined
control loops, fixed research phases, and native adaptation, allowing us
to examine runtime coordination across different native control
mechanisms. Each host’s native lifecycle serves as its N0 baseline.

### 4.2 Benchmark and Conditions

ResearchClawBench provides real-paper-derived tasks across scientific
domains. Each task supplies a research question, related literature, raw
data, and an executable environment while withholding the target
paper ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)). Our evaluation covers
mathematics, neuroscience, information science, energy, life science,
and physics. We evaluate Agent Laboratory and EvoScientist on ten tasks
each and ARK on five tasks. All runs use seed 0.

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Benchmark and Conditions ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
defines the cumulative conditions used to examine communication, runtime
selection, and contracts with verification. R3 versus N0 compares the
full framework with native execution; R2–R3 treats contracts and
verification as a joint addition rather than isolating their individual
effects.

[TABLE]

Table 1: Four cumulative conditions. R1 preserves native successors, R2
adds shared runtime selection, and R3 jointly adds scoped contracts and
verification.

### 4.3 Controls and Analysis

Within each host, we hold base models, native role prompts, tools,
permissions, artifact interfaces, and task inputs fixed across
conditions. Hop ceilings are calibrated to the corresponding host’s N0
hop count rather than set uniformly across hosts. The budget-matching
design concerns configured resource ceilings, not equal realized
consumption; routing and verification are charged to the run’s budget.
Budget accounting is described in
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Budget calibration and accounting ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?").
Cross-run memory and evolution stores are reset before each run to
isolate within-run coordination. Model choices and inference-cost
accounting are detailed in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?").

The primary outcome is the official ResearchClawBench weighted final
score. We report input and output token usage and estimated inference
costs separately. Each task–host–condition contributes one final score
from the consolidated results record, including numeric zeros. A zero is
an evaluator outcome, not an encoding of a missing report or a failed
evaluation. Within-task differences from N0 are averaged over the same
evaluated tasks within each host.
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Cumulative condition comparison ‣ 5 Results ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
provides task-level scores; all summaries use unrounded values before
display rounding.

### 5.3 Transferability Test

We additionally evaluated RAC on an exploratory subset of five
DiscoveryBench ([Majumder et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)) tasks, without a
predefined sampling rule. Agent Laboratory covers all five tasks;
EvoScientist covers only NLS SES, giving six task–host pairs rather than
a complete two-host matrix.
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Transferability Test ‣ 5 Results ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
shows mean improvements over N0 of 19.05, 18.07, and 25.92 points under
R1–R3, respectively. R3 achieved the largest aggregate gain, extending
the evaluation beyond ResearchClawBench without establishing
representative cross-benchmark performance.

R2’s slightly lower mean than R1 was driven by the incarceration and
archaeology tasks, despite improvements on the other three tasks. In
incarceration, R2 analyzed simulated data and reported synthetic year
indices rather than the requested survey years. In archaeology,
additional quantities in R2’s answer reduced the evaluator’s
variable-matching score, while relation and context matching remained
unchanged. Both runs completed the same six-stage sequence as R1 without
exhausting their budgets. These cases indicate task drift and scoring
sensitivity rather than a demonstrated disadvantage of runtime
selection.

### 5.4 Trace-level analysis: three coordination effects

We inspected 1,181 hop excerpts and 180 external scoring receipts from
the 60 cells covering five shared tasks, three hosts, and N0–R3.
Selected trajectories illustrate coordination mechanisms and failure
modes, not their prevalence or the causes of aggregate score
differences. The excerpts are incomplete, scientific claims were not
independently recomputed, and hop indices are zero-based.

#### Evidence–action closure effect.

In Physics-002 with EvoScientist R2, the native reviewer reported at
hop 6 that the report contained only 39 bytes despite existing code,
analyses, and figures. At hop 7, the selected debug capability reported
producing a 337-line report of approximately 22 KB. Ten recorded
scientific-artifact changes and the final inventory support the
conclusion that a report was produced. This handoff connected a specific
defect to corrective work, although subsequent debug calls made no
recorded scientific-artifact changes before the hop limit. The feedback
came from the host reviewer, not R3’s verifier; delivery repair does not
establish scientific correctness.

#### Planning stagnation after diagnosis.

In Physics-002 with EvoScientist R3, the reviewer identified a
standard-error discrepancy: 0.011 in the report versus 0.015 in the
data. At hop 8, the planner attributed it to duplicated observations and
proposed code changes followed by regeneration of results. However,
hops 8–13 remained planner calls with no recorded scientific-artifact
changes, ending at the 14-hop limit. The trajectory illustrates a
failure to move from diagnosis to implementation. Claims of repeated
verification appeared in agent messages but were not independently
confirmed from verifier events.

#### Self-consistent drift effect.

In Neuroscience-000 with EvoScientist R3, the native reviewer reported
that numerical and code–report consistency checks passed and assigned a
score of 8/10. External evaluation nevertheless identified missing
cross-laboratory, sex, and environment SHAP comparisons, yielding a
final score of 13.6. The two scores use different criteria and scales
and are not directly comparable. Similarly, Life-001 with Agent
Laboratory R2 analyzed ten synthetic patients rather than the supplied
seven-patient dataset. These cases distinguish internal consistency from
coverage of the research objective, without identifying whether
divergence originated in task interpretation, data limitations, or
coordination.

Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Detailed Case Studies of RAC Coordination ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
provides detailed trajectories and evidence boundaries, including
additional Math cases outside the shared-task subset.

## 6 Discussion

Runtime selection achieved the highest observed means on
ResearchClawBench, whereas contracts and verification produced the
largest aggregate gain on the exploratory DiscoveryBench subset. This
contrast suggests that the benefits of additional coordination depend on
the host and research setting, rather than increasing uniformly with
each mechanism.

Under matched budgets, communication and verification add context and
inference costs that may displace useful research work. Runtime
selection can offset this overhead by directing work toward relevant
agents, but R2’s lower recorded costs in ARK and Agent Laboratory did
not extend to EvoScientist. Additional budget might accommodate R3’s
overhead, yet the repeated planning trajectory in
Section [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Trace-level analysis: three coordination effects ‣ 5 Results ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
shows that diagnosis need not lead to implementation. Distracting
context or inaccurate verifier feedback could also weaken outcomes.
Budget sweeps with per-hop usage and artifact changes would help
distinguish resource constraints from ineffective delegation.

Host structure may further shape these trade-offs. Agent Laboratory’s
fixed phases may benefit from information carried between stages,
whereas EvoScientist already incorporates native adaptation. Differences
in native prompts and token consumption may also affect how effectively
hosts use additional context. These remain hypotheses: aggregate scores
and usage do not establish why individual runs improve or decline.

Our single-seed evaluation does not measure variability across
independent runs, and bounded benchmark tasks do not establish
performance in open-ended discovery. Costs are standardized token-based
estimates rather than provider invoices. R3 jointly adds contracts and
verification, so their individual effects remain unresolved.

## 7 Conclusion

We presented RAC as an alternative coordination approach for multi-agent
AI scientists. It selects existing agents from current state and, in R3,
adds scoped contracts and artifact-grounded verification feedback.
Across all available ResearchClawBench scores, R2 had the highest
task-weighted mean for each host, whereas R3’s performance relative to
N0 varied across hosts. These rankings are descriptive and do not
establish robustness across independent runs. Standardized token-based
costs describe resource use without establishing a general performance
or cost advantage.

### Ethics and reproducibility statement

Adaptive scientific workflows may accelerate research but can also
amplify unsupported claims or optimize for fallible reviewer signals.
RAC preserves host permissions, scopes tasks through contracts, and
records verification evidence, but verification is not a safety gate and
does not prevent unsupported outputs from propagating; accountable human
review remains necessary, particularly in safety-critical, dual-use, or
regulated domains. Sections 3 and 4 describe the host adaptation
boundary and experimental conditions,
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Cumulative condition comparison ‣ 5 Results ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
reports task-level scores,
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
specifies the execution and judge models and token-based cost
calculation, and
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Evaluation protocol ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
defines task weighting and the paired comparisons in
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Cumulative condition comparison ‣ 5 Results ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?").
The implementation is available at
[https://github.com/systemind-team/Runtime-AI-Scientist](https://github.com/systemind-team/Runtime-AI-Scientist).

## Appendix A Implementation Details

This appendix specifies the records that RAC writes during a run and the
boundary between RAC and each host. All conditions share the same RAC
package and condition configuration; only the host bridge differs across
hosts.

### A.1 Coordination records

Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ A.1 Coordination records ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
lists the records that document coordination decisions. Requests and
results are typed work.request and work.result events exchanged through
the common communication channel. R3 adds contracts and
work.verification records. Every verdict is retained and passed to the
next selected agent; no verdict discards the workspace or alters the
host transition.

[TABLE]

Table 5: Coordination records written by RAC. Checkpoints and event
records document coordination decisions; external benchmark evaluation
assesses final outputs separately.

### A.2 Host bridges and termination

Each host bridge serializes native state, invokes an existing
capability, and returns artifacts and usage records through a shared
interface. Bridges contain no host-specific runtime selection rules,
verification criteria, or benchmark hints, so each host keeps its
agents, tools, and permissions. Verification feedback enters the next
selected agent’s prompt rather than directly triggering retries,
rerouting, rollback, or stopping. Runs terminate on budget exhaustion,
hard hop limits, terminal provider errors, or native host completion.
Communication state is isolated between runs, and cross-run memory and
evolution stores are reset before each run.

## Appendix B Experimental Details

This appendix gives the models, budget calibration, cost accounting, and
evaluation protocol used for all reported comparisons.

### B.1 Models

We use DeepSeek V4 Pro as the execution model for the AI-scientist hosts
and GPT-5.5 as the external ResearchClawBench judge. External judging is
separate from the in-loop verifier and does not control agent selection
or host transitions.

### B.2 Budget calibration and accounting

Hop ceilings are tailored to each host using its N0 hop count as the
calibration reference. They are not a common cross-host constant: a
native phase may itself contain many model or tool calls. Configured
limits and realized usage must therefore be distinguished. Token and
call accounting includes coordination and verification, while external
judging is excluded. Limits checked after an agent returns can be
exceeded by that completed call; the excess is retained in usage totals,
and subsequent work is stopped.

The archived configurations contain multiple ceiling settings, and the
consolidated score table alone does not identify every final
configuration. We therefore do not infer a single numerical budget
vector for an entire host or equate the standardized USD estimates with
an enforced provider-spend limit. Budget matching describes the intended
comparison design, not an independently verified equality of every
archived resource ceiling. The results should be read as exploratory
comparisons rather than exact compute-equated effects.

### B.3 Cost accounting

We estimate inference costs from recorded input and output token usage
using a common DeepSeek V4 Pro tariff. We apply the official peak rates
of US\$1.32 per million non-cached input tokens and US\$3.96 per million
output tokens, as listed in the [DeepSeek API pricing
documentation](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing/) on 23
September 2026. For each episode, the estimated cost is
$`(1.32\,T_{\mathrm{in}}+3.96\,T_{\mathrm{out}})/10^{6}`$ USD. Here,
$`T_{\mathrm{in}}`$ and $`T_{\mathrm{out}}`$ are its recorded input and
output token counts. We apply no cache-hit or off-peak discounts. Table
entries average episode estimates before rounding. These are
standardized inference-cost estimates, not Azure invoices, and exclude
external GPT-5.5 judging charges.

### B.4 Evaluation protocol

The primary comparison is R3 versus N0 under matched budgets. Condition
means equally weight final task–host–condition scores. For each host and
each of R1–R3, we subtract the N0 score on the same task and average
these differences over the same evaluated task set within that host.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Cumulative condition comparison ‣ 5 Results ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
reports these descriptive paired means. The bars do not measure
variability across independent runs. Adjacent conditions are compared on
the same tasks, but R2–R3 does not separate contracts from verification.

in the main text.

### C.1 Token usage and estimated cost

summarizes mean input and output tokens and standardized inference costs
for the evaluated tasks. Agent Laboratory has its lowest input-token and
cost means in R2, but its lowest output-token mean in R1. EvoScientist
has its lowest token and cost means in N0. ARK has its lowest
input-token, output-token, and cost means in R2. These are within-host
resource summaries; the hosts use different task sets.

### C.4 ResearchClawBench criterion summaries

The descriptions below summarize what each criterion assesses. They
describe benchmark targets, not findings established by the evaluated
agents.

#### Neuroscience-000.

C1: attack-classifier precision–recall performance across conditions.
C2: cross-laboratory SHAP comparisons. C3: male–female SHAP comparisons.
C4: RI–CSDS environment SHAP comparisons. C5: permutation-based feature
importance.

#### Energy-001.

C1: construction of the Scottish wind-curtailment power-system model.
C2: constrained versus unconstrained optimal power flow. C3: dispatched
and curtailed wind over time. C4: loading of the Scotland–England
boundary link. C5: the open-source PyPSA-GB representation of the
British power system.

#### Life-001.

C1: immune-response distributions for optimized vaccines. C2: coverage
across response thresholds. C3: optimization runtime scaling. C4: recall
of experimentally validated neoantigens against ranking-based
comparators.

#### Neuroscience-002.

C1: FlyTracing dataset construction. C2: fusion of morphological and
image features. C3: EmbedNet weighting ablations. C4: robustness to
imaging artifacts. C5: visualization of neuron-segment embeddings.

#### Math-000.

C1: pseudo-depth estimation from image geometry. C2: depth cascade
matching using depth-partitioned association. C3: SparseTrack tracking
performance on MOT17, MOT20, and DanceTrack.

#### Math-001.

C1: accelerated convergence on a high-dimensional Lasso problem. C2:
convergence trajectories and stability-related evidence. C3: robustness
on an ill-conditioned regression problem.

#### Math-002.

C1: multi-agent path-finding performance in high-density settings. C2:
remaining collisions and solution cost. C3: zero-shot generalization
across map structures.

#### Math-003.

C1: geometry-proof performance on IMO-AG-30. C2: synthetic training-data
scale. C3: traceback-based identification of an unused premise and the
resulting theorem generalization.

#### Physics-002.

C1: fidelity scaling with qubit count at fixed depth. C2: fidelity
scaling with depth for 40 qubits. C3: depth-dependent fidelity estimates
for 56 qubits. C4: gate-counting predictions and uncertainty. C5:
counts-weighted linear XEB reproduction on the 40-qubit verification
subset.

#### Information-003.

C1: evidence connecting feature entanglement with detection failures.
C2: the DIDS-MFL disentanglement and graph-diffusion framework. C3:
few-shot intrusion-detection performance across benchmarks. C4:
component ablations and visualizations. C5: comparison with large
language models.

## Appendix D Detailed Case Studies of RAC Coordination

We examine five trajectories to illustrate how RAC changes the work
performed between agent boundaries. The cases cover direct reassignment
of corrective work, artifact-grounded verification without a change of
agent order, improved task relevance under communication-enabled
execution, and a failure to translate local completion into global
progress. We emphasize the concrete intervention visible in each trace:
which defect was identified, which capability acted next, what changed
on disk, and what the external judge subsequently assessed.

#### Evidence and interpretation.

These are selected qualitative cases, not additional controlled
ablations. The ARK records are exported hop summaries paired with
artifacts and external scoring receipts. The Math cases are identified
by individual episode records. Numerical outcomes refer to the final
scores reported in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Cumulative condition comparison ‣ 5 Results ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?");
older receipts are not used to decompose those scores. Their differences
describe the N0 and RAC executions, rather than isolated effects of a
coordination component. All hop indices are zero-based. Quoted passages
below reproduce short excerpts, with Markdown styling removed where
needed; the accompanying descriptions are our reconstruction from the
records, not additional agent dialogue. We distinguish the *host
reviewer*, which critiques research outputs, the *RAC verifier*, which
checks work-contract evidence, and the *external judge*, which applies
the benchmark criteria. We have not independently rerun the scientific
computations.

### D.1 ARK on Life-001: direct corrective handoffs

#### Outcome and coordination change.

The useful change in this R2 trajectory was a shorter path from a
concrete review finding to a revised artifact. Whereas the recorded
native successor after review was planner, RAC repeatedly selected
writer directly. This capability did more than edit prose: it reported
modifying analysis code, regenerating comparisons, and checking claims
against the underlying data. Thus, the observed benefit was not the
introduction of review—ARK already had a native review loop—but a change
in who acted immediately on its findings.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
2. Hop 4, writer: act directly on the implicated artifacts. The actual
next capability was writer. It reported adding
compute_greedy_minsum_curve() to the experiment code and regenerating a
figure with both curves, rather than merely renaming the existing
result. The export recorded 15 scientific-artifact changes at this hop.
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
3. Hop 5, reviewer: check the repair. The reviewer explicitly recognized
the added MinSum curve, threshold analysis, corrected coverage numbers,
and narrower claims. It then requested that replicate variability be
made visible and that clinical-feasibility language be qualified. 4. Hop
6, writer: complete the next local correction. RAC again selected the
writer directly. The report acquired the replicate-level range of mean
response probabilities, and claims of clinical feasibility were replaced
with claims about computational tractability at the tested scale. The
final report corroborates the central repair: it contains separate
greedy and MinSum coverage curves, with MinSum coverage of 97.9% at
budget four and 99.2% at budget ten. It also reports coverage at
multiple response thresholds rather than relying entirely on a single
cutoff. These persisted changes connect the selected capability to the
artifact that the reviewer had challenged.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
The revision replaced speculation about excluded vaccine elements with a
description grounded in those observations. This is a local
evidence–action closure: feedback specified a claim, the next capability
checked the relevant data, and the explanation changed.

#### Relation to the reported outcome.

Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Cumulative condition comparison ‣ 5 Results ‣ Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?")
reports final scores of 9.80 for N0 and 14.10 for R2, a difference of
4.30 points. The trace supports the local repairs described above, not a
quantitative attribution of the final score gain to individual handoffs.

The case nevertheless provides a concrete positive example of RAC
changing the native successor and closing local defects. Its boundary is
equally specific: efficacy experiments still used a single simulated
tumor with 100 cells per replicate, rather than the required
seven-patient, 10,000-cell analysis. The run also continued through
repeated revisions to the 46-hop limit. Direct corrective handoffs
improved a partially aligned study without completing the benchmark’s
broader scientific requirements.

#### Delivered-paper evidence: the correction survives into the manuscript.

The final paper explicitly separates the proposed objective from the
baseline and qualifies its comparative result:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This is more informative than a generic claim that a figure was fixed:
the delivered text identifies which curve represents MinSum and
distinguishes point-estimate differences from statistical superiority.
The paper also bounds the experiment:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The distinction prevents seven runtime instances from being read as
seven independent efficacy studies. These passages support the positive
interpretation of the trace: corrective handoffs improved the fidelity
and qualification of the delivered comparison, even though they did not
supply the missing patient-scale evaluation.

#### Residual inconsistency: repaired delivery does not certify the objective.

The same paper defines a minimization objective that decomposes as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}(S)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log(1-P_{i}(S))=\sum_{j\in S}w_{j},\qquad w_{j}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log(1-p_{ij}),
``` |  |

but its accompanying instruction reads:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For the stated minimization of a sum of fixed weights, the selected
weights should instead be the smallest ones. This establishes a
contradiction in the paper’s description, not that the implementation
necessarily used the wrong order. The paper also acknowledges that this
is “structurally the same ranking paradigm the Introduction critiques”.
Consequently, the corrected comparison is evidence of improved
reporting, not evidence of a newly established combinatorial
optimization paradigm. RAC’s observed success here is local: it closes
particular reviewer-identified defects while leaving a mathematical
description that warrants further checking.

### D.2 ARK on Physics-002: repair followed by cross-capability checking

#### Outcome and coordination change.

The selected R3 snapshot scored 34.6, compared with 27.6 for N0. RAC
departed from the recorded native successor at several boundaries and
assigned concrete defects across writer, coder, and experimenter
capabilities. The resulting trajectory is useful because it includes
both a correction to existing evidence and a second check that caught an
error introduced while extending a figure.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
The recorded successor was planner. 2. Hop 8, writer: revise before
replanning. RAC selected writer instead. The writer added the N56 table,
disclosed 100 shots per instance at depth 24 versus 20 at other depths,
and corrected a caption that described a nonexistent second axis. 3. Hop
9, coder: inspect the partially repaired report. Rather than proceeding
directly to the writer’s proposed reviewer successor, execution moved to
coder. It verified the seven XEB depth values and found a residual
discrepancy between the discussion and conclusion:
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
4. Hop 10, experimenter: check against numerical artifacts. The
experimenter checked the XEB values against the instance records and
reported a maximum discrepancy of 0.00028, within the stated rounding
tolerance. It also corrected Transport confidence intervals and added
the corresponding N56 table. The final report contains the corrected
depth-10 XEB value of 0.450. The significance statements in these
excerpts remain agent calculations, not independent validation by our
audit; the directly checked fact is that the handoff led to
reconciliation of the persisted report and its cited outputs.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
The depth-24 data used 100 shots per instance, not 20. The experimenter
reported changing the interval from $`[0.1014,0.1428]`$ to
$`[0.1119,0.1302]`$. The final report both references panel (c) and
records the rounded corrected interval $`[0.112,0.130]`$, together with
100 shots per instance and 5,000 total trials. This sequence links a
scoped figure task to implementation, a distinct checking step, and a
corrected delivered result.

#### RAC’s contribution and its scope.

The archived provenance for this ARK R3 case identifies an
expanded-budget continuation. We therefore use its trace as qualitative
evidence of local repairs, not as a matched-budget estimate of their
benefit. Unlike a fixed traversal of role names, the observed routing
followed the type of outstanding work: document reconciliation, code and
figure repair, and numerical checking. Typed issue identifiers in the
summaries made the requested changes concrete. The cross-capability
check was productive because it found a specific new bug, not merely
because a second agent declared the work complete. The export does not
include the underlying RAC verifier ledger for these ARK hops, so this
example establishes a corrective handoff pattern rather than
independently verified contract compliance at every boundary.

N0’s report had introduced an additional “unbiased XEB” rescaling,
whereas R3 retained values on the target scale. This between-run method
difference must not be mistaken for a logged repair of N0’s code by R3.
The within-R3 evidence above instead shows how concrete inconsistencies
were repaired and checked before delivery; it does not decompose the
7.0-point final-score difference. Gate-counting uncertainty bands and
the required mirror-circuit inference remained incomplete.

#### Delivered-paper evidence: a correct patch and an obsolete claim coexist.

The final manuscript provides unusually direct evidence of both the
value and the limits of local repair. Its comparison paragraph retains
the following sentence:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Yet the same paragraph subsequently states:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The table supports the latter values: the depth-12 difference is only
0.019, compared with 0.068 and 0.063 at depths 10 and 16. The
corresponding intervals also overlap at those depths, so the “within-CI”
qualification does not resolve the obsolete superlative. Both sentences
occur in the original main.tex, not only in the Markdown export. A
corrected statement was delivered without fully reconciling the
surrounding text.

The figure repair is more cleanly reflected in the final artifact. The
paper reports the depth-24 pooled interval as $`[0.112,0.130]`$, and its
table lists 100 shots per instance and 5,000 total trials. These are the
quantities implicated in the hop-43 denominator correction. Thus, the
paper corroborates a successful numerical patch while exposing a
separate synchronization failure. The mechanism-level lesson is not that
cross-capability checking failed altogether, but that checking a named
value or figure can succeed without checking every dependent statement
in the manuscript. The higher score and the remaining contradiction can
therefore coexist.

### D.3 EvoScientist on Math-001: explicit delivery verification with unchanged agent order

#### Outcome and coordination change.

The selected R3 episode scored 37.7, compared with 16.8 for N0. Its
executed sequence remained planner, research, code, debug, data
analysis, and writing. This case therefore illustrates a different RAC
contribution: a work contract distinguished an agent’s nonempty response
from an actual implementation, even though the next agent retained the
native position in the workflow.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
3. Hop 2, RAC verifier. The actual evaluation event recorded
nonempty_output: passed, artifact_changed: failed, and verdict refuted:
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
4. Hop 3, debug invocation. The next capability delivered the missing
implementation rather than only commenting on it. Its output began:
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
The artifact record includes solver modules, a Lasso experiment,
convergence plots, and method-comparison results. The subsequent
verifier event recorded supported and listed the changed code and output
files.

#### Why this is a useful positive contract example.

RAC added an explicit, machine-recorded distinction between *intention
to perform work* and *evidence that the work was delivered*. That
distinction exposed a gap that a nonempty-output check alone would have
missed. The following native debug capability then filled the gap, after
which analysis and writing produced a substantive report. Thus, a
visibly unchanged agent order did not imply unchanged coordination
semantics: the boundary now carried an auditable delivery verdict.

The scope of the inference matters. The code invocation had already
proposed debug as its successor; the trace does not show a
verifier-induced reroute, forced retry, or rollback. Nor does this
single trajectory isolate whether debug would have repaired the missing
implementation without the advisory. The supported observation is the
sequence of explicit detection followed by artifact-backed recovery,
which is consistent with a beneficial role for contracts and
verification without changing the agent roster or order.

#### Relation to the result.

The N0 receipt describes a VOS method that underperformed its baseline;
the R3 submission provided a more complete implementation, comparator
analysis, convergence evidence, and a 460-line report. These differences
explain why the external judge had more relevant evidence to assess,
while the trace identifies a concrete delivery gap successfully closed
along the way. The result was still partial: the run exceeded its
input-token budget after writing, before a native review invocation, and
did not fully establish the requested convergence target. The 20.9-point
difference is therefore an outcome associated with this recovered
trajectory, not a measured causal effect of the verifier alone.

#### Delivered-paper evidence: a working comparator, not a new winning algorithm.

The generated paper explicitly characterizes the implemented method as
matching an established baseline:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Its comparison table gives both FISTA and VOS 92 iterations, with fitted
rates of 6.60 and 6.61, respectively. This grounds the positive case
more precisely: the recovered implementation supplies a functioning
accelerated baseline and relevant comparison evidence. It does not
demonstrate a distinct algorithm outperforming FISTA. That narrower
interpretation is consistent with the delivery contract: the missing
implementation was supplied, but the verifier did not establish
algorithmic novelty.

#### Residual numerical and theoretical overreach.

Two passages show why artifact-backed delivery must be distinguished
from validation of the scientific conclusions. First, the paper states:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The comparison table instead lists final suboptimalities of
$`1.40\times 10^{-5}`$ for FISTA, $`1.40\times 10^{-6}`$ for ADMM, and
$`1.37\times 10^{-5}`$ for VOS. If these use a common reference optimum,
the FISTA–ADMM objective difference is approximately
$`1.26\times 10^{-5}`$, inconsistent with the quoted tolerance. If
different references were used, the paper would need to explain how the
cross-method claim was obtained. We flag an unreconciled reporting
discrepancy rather than claim to have recomputed the objectives.

Second, the paper’s Lyapunov diagnostic uses changing reference values:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The discussion acknowledges that “the dynamic update of $`f^{\star}`$
and $`x^{\star}`$ introduces reference-point shifts”, but the conclusion
nevertheless describes the experiment as “exhibiting the predicted
Lyapunov monotonicity (85.9% monotonic steps, $`p=2.87`$ decay
exponent)”. A moving-reference, partly non-monotone diagnostic is not a
direct verification of a fixed-reference monotonicity theorem. Nor do
these discrete observations by themselves refute a continuous-time
theorem. The appropriate claim is evidence of empirical decay under the
implemented diagnostic. This separates RAC’s observable
contribution—detecting and closing a delivery gap—from stronger
mathematical claims that its artifact checks did not validate.

### D.4 Agent Laboratory on Math-003: greater task relevance under communication-enabled execution

#### Outcome and coordination condition.

The selected R1 episode scored 10.05, compared with 0 for N0. N0 studied
an unrelated synthetic-transformation setup. R1 instead developed a
geometry-proof experiment with self-play and comparison baselines.
Because R1 preserved the native successor and did not enable
work-contract verification, this case examines improvement under
communication-enabled execution rather than dynamic selection or
verifier-guided repair.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
The workflow retained literature review, plan formulation, data
preparation, experiments, interpretation, and report writing. Evaluation
events explicitly stated that verification was disabled. 2. Hop 1, plan
formulation. The planning dialogue framed proof steps as actions in a
geometry-solving system, combining sequence generation, search, and
self-play. Its stated goal was:
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
3. Hop 3, experiments. Execution attempted the task-relevant
experimental plan, encountering several 600-second code-execution
timeouts and native repair attempts before producing results. These
repairs belong to the host’s internal execution machinery, not to an R3
verifier. 4. Hop 4, interpretation. The next stage discussed the actual
failures of that experiment rather than substituting a different
research question:
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
5. Hop 5, writing. A report of the geometry experiment was delivered.
Input-token exhaustion prevented the subsequent refinement stage.

#### The communication-related interpretation.

The positive change was continuity of a relevant research objective
across planning, implementation, and interpretation. Under the
communication-enabled condition, the host produced a connected, albeit
unsuccessful, geometry experiment instead of an off-task study. This
motivates communication as a way of improving what successive agents
coordinate around without changing their order. However, the recorded
host dialogue is not itself proof of SharedNet message consumption. The
available evidence does not link a particular SharedNet message to a
downstream decision, and R1 differs from N0 in its integration context
as well as communication availability. We therefore treat this as a
communication-consistent example, not a component-level causal
demonstration.

The score increase should also be read as improved relevance, not
improved theorem-proving performance: every reported method solved 0 of
the ten evaluated problems, and the study did not reproduce the full
target benchmark. Planning consumed approximately 70.5% of the episode’s
recorded input tokens. The trajectory shows the value of preserving a
meaningful task across handoffs, while also showing that relevance alone
does not ensure successful execution or efficient use of the budget.

#### Delivered-paper evidence: relevant and candid negative results.

The R1 manuscript reports the failure directly rather than manufacturing
successful proof results:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

It positions its contribution accordingly:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The latter is an excerpt from a longer sentence. Together, these
passages reinforce the positive but limited interpretation: R1 delivered
an on-topic experiment and openly reported unsuccessful outcomes. The
relevance gain does not depend on accepting the manuscript’s explanation
of those outcomes.

#### Code evidence: the failure explanation misses implementation-level causes.

The paper interprets a zero supervised loss as successful memorization:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

However, the delivered training loop constructs its legal-action mask
from the target action alone. The following contiguous excerpt is from
run_experiments.py:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The forward pass masks other logits, and the loss is cross-entropy
against that same target. With only the target class left available,
probability one and a near-zero loss follow from the mask; they are not
evidence that the network learned to distinguish competing actions. This
static implementation evidence supports a more specific explanation than
memorization.

The immediate self-play reward has a similarly concrete cause. In
random_provable_problem(), the generator repeatedly applies a theorem
and updates state = ns. It then sets the goal to the conclusion of the
last applied theorem and returns that already-expanded state, rather
than the original premises. The decisive terminal statements are:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The theorem application has already inserted its conclusion into the
state’s relations; the goal check tests membership in those relations.
When there is no recorded application, the alternative branch chooses an
existing relation as the goal. Thus, the returned training instance
already contains its goal. This explains why immediate success can occur
without a learned proof policy. The paper instead discusses forward
chaining as producing goals reachable “in zero or one steps”, framing
the problem primarily as an overly easy curriculum.

These are static code findings, not results of a rerun or proof that
fixing the two issues would solve the benchmark. They identify a missed
distinction between a genuinely informative negative experiment and an
implementation artifact. R1 improved task continuity and reporting
relevance, but did not provide the semantic checking needed to catch
these defects before they became an explanatory narrative. Since
verification was disabled in R1, this is not a failed R3 verifier
verdict.

### D.5 EvoScientist on Math-003: local contracts can leave the global objective unfinished

#### Outcome and failure boundary.

The selected R3 episode scored 9.7, below the N0 score of 16.3. This is
not a case in which RAC broke an otherwise successful prover: N0 also
reported 0/30 solved problems. The useful contrast is that R3 developed
and validated a narrower intermediate artifact, then proceeded to
analyze and write about it while the planned system remained incomplete.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
It reported 89 passing tests and successful parsing of all 30 problems.
The contract’s executable evidence checks required changed code/result
artifacts and nonempty output; the RAC verifier returned supported. 3.
Hop 3, debug. Debugging fixed five reported bugs and increased the test
count to 102. These were genuine local improvements to the implemented
foundation. 4. Hop 4, data analysis. Instead of returning to the
unimplemented neural and search components, execution moved to analysis
of the existing artifact: relation counts, predicate distributions, and
related diagnostics, with 11 generated figures. Its contract also
received supported. 5. Hops 5–6, writing and host review. The writer
produced an 861-line report centered on Stage 0. The host reviewer gave
8/10 after checking such properties as the passing tests and the
reported 0/30 result. All seven RAC verification events in the episode
were supported.

#### What the negative case says about RAC.

The verification results were compatible with their local evidence
rules: files changed, outputs were nonempty, and the parser was tested.
The weakness was the connection between those local checks and the
remaining scientific obligations. The contract objective named
autonomous geometry solving, but its executable criteria did not
establish that the full planned solver had been implemented. Runtime
selection continued along the native sequence, allowing analysis and
writing to consolidate the partial system rather than return to the
missing stages.

This illustrates a failure mode in which locally supported work
accumulates without closing the global objective. RAC made the
intermediate work explicit and checkable, but did not prevent premature
progression from a useful foundation to a final report. The episode
ultimately exceeded its input-token limit; nevertheless, the narrowing
to Stage 0 was already visible before termination. Budget exhaustion
alone therefore does not explain the observed sequence. The case
motivates connecting contracts and subsequent selection to unresolved
end-to-end requirements, rather than interpreting supported as
scientific completion. It does not establish that contracts necessarily
caused the narrowing or generally reduce performance.

#### Delivered-paper evidence: the missing system becomes future work.

The final manuscript makes the gap between local completion and the
research objective explicit. It reports:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Elsewhere, it describes its foundation in stronger terms:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Handling the input representation and passing local tests are compatible
with solving none of the benchmark problems, but “handles … correctly”
should not be read as end-to-end proof success. Likewise, the observed
0/30 is a result for this implementation and configuration; it does not
establish a general impossibility result for forward chaining. The
paper’s appeal to the upstream system’s performance does not validate
the completeness of its own reproduction.

Most revealingly, the manuscript’s “Next Steps (Stage 1–5)” section
places the planned core components after the delivered study: “Synthetic
Data Generation”, “GNN Architecture and Training”, “MCTS Integration”,
“Self-Play Expert Iteration”, and “Evaluation”. The proposed MCTS
success criterion is to solve at least three of the 30 problems within
10,000 simulations. This is a future target, not an achieved result. The
paper therefore corroborates the trace more strongly than a low score
alone: the planned learning-and-search system was explicitly deferred
while the foundation was packaged as the final contribution.

RAC’s local contracts did capture real work—parser repairs, tests, and
diagnostic artifacts—but their supported verdicts did not keep the
missing stages active as prerequisites for final delivery. The negative
case is consequently about the granularity and coverage of coordination
obligations, not the uselessness of the intermediate work. A polished
account of an incomplete system can satisfy local delivery checks while
losing external credit for the actual research objective.

#### Cross-case synthesis.

The two ARK trajectories illustrate altered corrective handoffs that
produced observable repairs. EvoScientist on Math-001 shows how delivery
verification can distinguish a missing implementation from a nonempty
response without changing the next agent. Agent Laboratory on Math-003
shows greater task relevance under communication-enabled fixed-order
execution, with weaker evidence for the communication mechanism itself.
The final case bounds these benefits: artifact-level success must remain
connected to the unfinished research objective. Together, the cases
locate RAC’s potential value at the interfaces between agents—what
evidence is handed over, what obligation is assigned, and what work
follows—rather than in the number of agents invoked or the presence of a
positive local verdict.

## Appendix E Condensed All-Hop Trajectories

We summarize all 92 exported hops from Physics-002 / ARK / R3 and
Life-001 / ARK / R2, retaining one row per hop and the chronological
order. The tables condense reported work, corrective handoffs, and
repeated checking; selected complete exported summaries follow. Phase
headings are editorial groupings, not additional workflow stages.

#### Reading the tables.

Work descriptions paraphrase agent-reported actions; they do not
independently validate scientific results. In the final column,
*recorded next* is the successor specified by the host’s native
workflow, whereas *observed next* is the agent selected by RAC and
actually invoked next. Blue entries highlight departures from the native
successor; the record alone does not establish the rationale for each
selection. Res., Exp., Wri., Rev., Plan., and Code denote researcher,
experimenter, writer, reviewer, planner, and coder. A dash means no
subsequent hop is exported. The host reviewer is distinct from the RAC
verifier and the external benchmark judge.

These are qualitative records, not isolated estimates of causal benefit
or matched-budget efficiency. The boxes following each table preserve
selected complete exported summaries. Internal ratings are not external
benchmark scores. Markdown syntax is retained as text, with typography
and emoji markers adapted for print.

## Appendix F Generative AI Use Disclosure

Generative AI systems are intrinsic experimental components of the
evaluated AI-scientist workflows. They generate plans, code,
experimental analyses, reviews, and manuscript drafts inside each
evaluated system. Human authors are responsible for the research
question, system design, evaluation protocol, verification of reported
values, literature checking, interpretation, and final manuscript. All
AI-assisted content was checked against persisted artifacts and source
records before submission.
````
